doc.title: Denny Zeitlin interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Paul Winter brings him to John Hammond at Columbia
summary: In 1963 Paul Winter dragged him to play for John Hammond, who offered him a Columbia contract.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: So I didn’t have big aspirations to record. All through college, I went to the University of Illinois where there were lots of opportunities to play with good people, I mean Jack McDuff was down there, Wes Montgomery was living in Danville at the time and I used to do some sessions with him and a wonderful tenor player named Punchy Atkinson, Joe Farintello, who changed his name to Joe Farrell, the tenor player who died all too young, a wonderful player. Roger Kellaway was playing bass then in and around the University of Illinois. So there was opportunity to play with a lot of good cats. And then when I went to medical school at Johns Hopkins in Baltimore, which was in 1960, I continued to get a chance to play and sit in in places. There was a place called the North End Lounge that was owned by Gary Bartz’s father. So I started sitting in there typically on weekends and sometimes even during the week and playing with Gary. I just loved Gary’s playing. And there were some wonderful players that used to play with him. So I got a chance to sit in and keep the music moving along. And then everything really changed dramatically in terms of a step into a more public kind of musical life in 1963. I had a fellowship at Columbia University in psychiatry, a ten-week fellowship. And so I was living in a little apartment that I was just renting for that time. And Paul Winter, who I had known from back in Chicago and had heard me play and liked my playing, who had just recently begun to record for Columbia, and he wanted to get together and I was visiting him at his place and he said, “Denny, I want you to play for my producer at Columbia, John

Hammond, he’s a really wonderful guy. I’d just like to have him hear you play.” I said, “oh, Paul, I don’t want to get into that stuff. I really don’t want to mess with you.” “Come on, Hammond is different than all the rest.”
Yeah? Did you know John Hammond’s name at the time?
No. I didn’t know the significance until Paul then told me that he had discovered Benny Goodman and who else, Basie.
And Dylan later and all that.

Yeah. Billie Holiday, Springsteen. So many folks. So sort of kicking and screaming he dragged me to Columbia to play for John Hammond. And so I played a few tunes and he said, “gee I really love what you play, I’d love for you to record for Columbia, you can come on in and play whatever you want, use whomever you want.” And at that time I didn’t know how extraordinarily lucky and unusual that was, so I just sort of slipped into recording in 1963, and so because Columbia was a powerful label and it got a lot of distribution and exposure, it just opened up a whole bunch of stuff for me overnight. So I might never have recorded perhaps if Paul Winter hadn’t grabbed me by the ear and dragged me into his office.
